name: Titus
description: Tested leaders · household care · grace · good work · shared support

1.text: Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God’s chosen ones and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness,
in hope of eternal life, which God, who can’t lie, promised before time began;
but in his own time revealed his word in the message with which I was entrusted according to the commandment of God our Savior,
to Titus, my true child according to a common faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior.
I left you in Crete for this reason, that you would set in order the things that were lacking and appoint elders in every city, as I directed you—
if anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having children who believe, who are not accused of loose or unruly behavior.
For the overseer must be blameless, as God’s steward, not self-pleasing, not easily angered, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for dishonest gain;
but given to hospitality, a lover of good, sober minded, fair, holy, self-controlled,
holding to the faithful word which is according to the teaching, that he may be able to exhort in the sound doctrine, and to convict those who contradict him.
For there are also many unruly men, vain talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision,
whose mouths must be stopped: men who overthrow whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for dishonest gain’s sake.
One of them, a prophet of their own, said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, and idle gluttons.”
This testimony is true. For this cause, reprove them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,
not paying attention to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn away from the truth.
To the pure, all things are pure, but to those who are defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their mind and their conscience are defiled.
They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him, being abominable, disobedient, and unfit for any good work.

2.text: But say the things which fit sound doctrine,
that older men should be temperate, sensible, sober minded, sound in faith, in love, and in perseverance,
and that older women likewise be reverent in behavior, not slanderers nor enslaved to much wine, teachers of that which is good,
that they may train the young wives to love their husbands, to love their children,
to be sober minded, chaste, workers at home, kind, being in subjection to their own husbands, that God’s word may not be blasphemed.
Likewise, exhort the younger men to be sober minded.
In all things show yourself an example of good works. In your teaching, show integrity, seriousness, incorruptibility,
and soundness of speech that can’t be condemned, that he who opposes you may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say about us.
Exhort servants to be in subjection to their own masters and to be well-pleasing in all things, not contradicting,
not stealing, but showing all good fidelity, that they may adorn the doctrine of God, our Savior, in all things.
For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men,
instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age;
looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ,
who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works.
Say these things and exhort and reprove with all authority. Let no one despise you.

3.text: Remind them to be in subjection to rulers and to authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work,
to speak evil of no one, not to be contentious, to be gentle, showing all humility toward all men.
For we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared,
not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,
whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior;
that being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

This saying is faithful, and concerning these things I desire that you insist confidently, so that those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable to men;
but shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
Avoid a factious man after a first and second warning,
knowing that such a one is perverted and sinful, being self-condemned.
When I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, be diligent to come to me to Nicopolis, for I have determined to winter there.
Send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey speedily, that nothing may be lacking for them.
Let our people also learn to maintain good works to meet necessary needs, that they may not be unfruitful.
All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in faith. Grace be with you all. Amen.

chapters.title: Tested conduct and sound teaching must answer disruption within households
chapters.summary: The letter is addressed from Paul to Titus, his true child in faith. Paul left Titus in Crete to appoint elders in every city. An elder must be blameless, the husband of one wife, with believing children. An overseer must not be self-pleasing, quick to anger, violent, or greedy. He must be hospitable, self-controlled, and hold to the faithful word. Many unruly talkers upset whole households for dishonest gain. The letter quotes a Cretan saying against Cretans. Titus is to rebuke them sharply.
chapters.meaning: Verses 6–8 describe an elder’s home and character. Verse 9 adds what he must do with the teaching. He must hold to the faithful word as he was taught. That gives him two abilities. He can encourage with sound doctrine, and he can refute those who contradict. Verses 10–11 show why both are needed in Crete. Teachers there upset whole households, and their mouths must be stopped.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches sound doctrine as protection against false instruction. Why does a teacher's conduct matter when whole households face disruption?

chapters.historicalNote: The greeting connects knowledge of truth with godliness before describing Titus's unfinished work on Crete. Elders need tested household conduct because care for the assembly includes responsibility toward dependent people. Anger, violence, and greed would contradict the trust required for that care. The opposing teachers threaten whole households, so correction concerns consequences rather than disagreement alone. The quoted insult against Cretans serves the letter's accusation rather than establishing every inhabitant's character. The final contrast tests claims to know God against deeds that make those claims empty.
chapters.mapNote: Where Crete appears, the map marks it as one island point. Nicopolis has no point.
chapters.routeEvidence: The letter gives no travel route.

chapters.title: Grace supplies the reason for instruction and eagerness to do good
chapters.summary: Titus is to teach what fits sound doctrine. Older men are to be sober and sound in faith. Older women are to teach the younger to love their husbands and children. Young men are to be self-controlled, and Titus is to be their example. Servants are to please their masters and not steal. The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all. It trains people to live soberly while they wait for Christ’s appearing. He gave himself to redeem a people eager for good works.
chapters.meaning: Verses 2–10 give instructions to five groups in the household. Verse 11 begins with “for” and gives the ground: God’s grace has appeared. Verse 12 says grace trains people to deny ungodliness and live soberly. Verse 14 names the act behind that grace. Christ “gave himself for us.” Two purposes follow: to redeem from all iniquity and to purify a people. That people is marked by one trait: zeal for good works.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches sound doctrine as protection against false instruction. How does grace supply the reason for good work within these unequal instructions?

chapters.historicalNote: Directions to older and younger people organize teaching through relationships within the household. Older women receive a teaching role, while wives and bound workers receive unequal instructions. The repeated concern about outsiders' judgment explains why visible behavior matters to the argument. Pietz reads grace as the basis for good work rather than self-improvement alone. Grace also instructs present conduct while the hearers wait for the promised appearing of Christ. His self-giving creates a people eager to do good rather than merely avoid criticism.

Verse 12 says grace trains people to deny ungodliness and live soberly. Verse 14 names the act behind that grace. chapters.title: Received mercy directs attention from disputes toward work that meets needs
chapters.summary: Titus is to remind them to obey rulers and be gentle to all. The writers too were once foolish, disobedient, and hateful. Then God’s kindness appeared, and he saved them by mercy, not by their works. He did it through washing and renewal by the Holy Spirit. Those who believe should be careful to do good works. Titus should avoid foolish disputes and reject a divisive person after two warnings. Paul will send Artemas or Tychicus and asks Titus to come to Nicopolis. He should help Zenas and Apollos on their journey.
chapters.meaning: Verses 4–7 say God saved by mercy and not by works done in righteousness. Verse 8 calls this a faithful saying and tells Titus to insist on it. The purpose is that believers be careful to do good works. Works do not earn the mercy; they follow it. The verse calls them good and profitable to people. Verse 9 names the contrast: disputes about the law are unprofitable. Verse 14 gives the practical form: good works that meet pressing needs.

lds.text: How do the closing travel requests make useful work concrete?

chapters.historicalNote: The opening requires gentle conduct toward others under rulers and authorities. Remembered foolishness prevents believers from treating former failures as belonging only to outsiders. God's kindness and mercy then explain salvation rather than earlier achievements that earned it. This account makes good work a response to received grace instead of its purchase price. Repeated disputes cannot replace that response, and warnings limit the treatment of a divisive person. The closing travel requests make useful work concrete through care for workers who need support.

people.name: Paul
people.role: Writer who leaves Titus on Crete to set things in order
people.relations: He calls Titus a true child in their common faith.
people.meaning: Paul says he left Titus on Crete to appoint elders in every city. He lists what an elder must be. He warns of deceivers who overthrow whole houses. He tells Titus to reprove them sharply. He then asks Titus to meet him at Nicopolis.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Jesus Christ
people.role: Savior whose grace and gift are the reason for good work
people.relations: Paul calls him Savior and our great God and Savior. Paul says he gave himself for us.
people.meaning: Paul says Jesus gave himself to redeem us from all iniquity. He says God saved us through mercy, and not by our works. Paul then asks his people to keep up good works.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Titus
people.role: Paul’s true child, told to appoint elders on Crete
people.relations: Paul calls him his true child in a common faith. Paul asks him to come to Nicopolis.
people.meaning: Paul left Titus on Crete to appoint elders and set things in order. Paul tells him to teach each group what fits sound doctrine. Paul tells him to remind them to do good works. Paul asks him to come to Nicopolis once Artemas or Tychicus arrives.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Tychicus
people.role: Worker Paul may send to Titus
people.relations: Paul says he will send Artemas or Tychicus to Titus.
people.meaning: Paul says he will send Artemas or Tychicus to Titus. Then Titus is to come to Paul at Nicopolis. The letter does not say which of the two Paul sends.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

people.name: Apollos
people.role: Traveler Titus must send on his journey
people.relations: Paul names him with Zenas the lawyer.
people.meaning: Paul tells Titus to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey. He must do it quickly. Nothing may be lacking for them.
people.life: Birth and death years are not securely known.

places.name: Crete
places.summary: Paul left Titus on Crete in chapter 1. Titus is to appoint elders in every city there. Paul warns him about deceivers on the island.
places.limits: Crete is an island. The letter names no town or meeting place on it.
